title: EXPLORE ONGOING SUPPORT OR COACHING WITH CHATGPT
content:
Ongoing support or coaching sits naturally near both subscriptions and services. The label matters less than understanding what the customer is paying to keep receiving.

If they are primarily paying for continued access, guidance, accountability, or support, the subscription framing may be useful. If they are primarily paying you to perform recurring work for them, the service branch may describe the business more clearly.

CONTINUING ACCESS CAN BE THE PRODUCT
Customers may want regular feedback, accountability, expert interpretation, office hours, check-ins, or access when questions arise rather than a single completed task.

WATCH CAPACITY
Recurring revenue is not automatically scalable revenue. If every subscriber receives an hour of your personal time each week, adding subscribers adds fulfillment quickly. Define access and capacity clearly.

KNOW WHEN THIS IS REALLY A SERVICE
If the customer mainly pays you to perform recurring work, such as monthly bookkeeping, the service branch may describe the business more usefully.

CAPACITY EXAMPLE
A $100/month support membership with one private hour per member each week may sound like recurring revenue. Ten members could also require roughly forty private hours per month before preparation, messages, administration, and other work.

Changing the offer to group calls, office hours, limited asynchronous support, or another structure changes both the customer experience and capacity. Define the value before deciding which structure is appropriate.

WHEN ONGOING SUPPORT BECOMES A SUBSCRIPTION-LIKE OFFER

Suppose someone pays $100 each month for access to a weekly group question-and-answer call plus a resource library.

They are not paying off a finished product. They keep paying because access to ongoing help remains useful.

Now suppose someone pays $100 each month for you to personally reconcile their accounts and prepare a bookkeeping report. That is recurring revenue too, but the value comes primarily from new work you perform for that individual customer. The service branch is a better description.

The line can blur. A coaching membership may include some individualized help. A service may include access to resources or support between appointments.

Use the dominant promise. If the customer is mainly buying continued ACCESS to guidance that can serve multiple customers, this branch may fit. If they are mainly buying repeated individualized WORK, think of it as a recurring service.

WHY CAPACITY STILL MATTERS

Ongoing support is not automatically scalable. If every new subscriber expects an hour of private help each week, the subscription can behave like a service with a recurring invoice.

Ask what one additional customer requires from you. That question reveals whether the model can serve more people without your delivery time increasing at the same rate.

WHAT YOU SHOULD DECIDE HERE

Choose this direction when customers benefit from continued access to your help and that access can be structured in a way you actually want to deliver.

Be specific about the access.

A monthly group call is different from unlimited messaging. Office hours are different from private weekly sessions. Feedback on submitted work is different from doing the work for the customer.

Those choices determine both customer value and your capacity.

If every subscriber creates substantial individualized work, you may really be designing a recurring service. That is fine. Classifying it accurately helps you understand what growth will require.

HOW TO USE THIS
Use the prompt below to turn this branch into your version of the business. Answer the questions honestly, ask for clarification when you need it, and do not treat external facts as verified just because ChatGPT mentions them.

WHAT THIS INTERVIEW SHOULD PRODUCE

By the end, you should have a specific ongoing-support promise, clear access boundaries, a delivery structure, and a rough understanding of how customer count affects your time.

ChatGPT should ask what "access to me" actually means.

If every subscriber requires substantial individualized work, it should say that the model behaves like a recurring service even if it is billed as a subscription.

COPY & PASTE INTO CHATGPT

During the interview:
- Ask one question at a time unless a small group of tightly related questions is genuinely easier to answer together.
- Use my answers before deciding what to ask next. Do not run through a generic questionnaire when an answer makes a question irrelevant.
- If I say "I don't know," help me identify what I need to decide or research. Do not silently invent an answer for me.
- Explain unfamiliar business terms in plain language when they first become relevant.
- Separate assumptions from facts that require outside verification.
- Do not turn this into a marketing or customer-acquisition plan unless the purpose of this specific interview requires it.
- When you have enough information, stop interviewing me and give me the requested conclusion, including the important unknowns and next research questions.
Ask me one question at a time unless a small group of closely related questions would be easier to answer together. If I say I don't know, help me identify what I would need to decide or research instead of inventing an answer for me.

Interview me about an ongoing support or coaching idea. Ask who it serves, the continuing problem or result, why support needs to continue, what kind of access I would provide, whether delivery is individual or group, frequency, boundaries, capacity, and what happens between interactions.

Help me decide whether the primary value is continued access/support or recurring work performed for the customer. Flag professional licensing, credentials, scope-of-practice issues, insurance, legal terms, taxes, and demand for independent verification where relevant.

End with a specific recurring support/coaching direction and explain which framing fits it best.

NEXT → PDF 46 if clear; PDF 39 if it is really a service; PDF 32 to reconsider.

While interviewing me, follow these rules:

Distinguish continuing access from recurring task fulfillment. If the user is mostly describing work done for each client, explicitly compare the service branch.

Do not ignore capacity just because billing is recurring.

At the end, give me:
- Customer
- Continuing need
- Type and limits of access/support
- Delivery frequency
- Individual/group structure
- Capacity estimate questions
- Professional verification needs
- Best framing: subscription-style support or recurring service
- Specific direction
